Empirical Research Plan  
“Medicaid, Work, and the Safety Net: Evidence from Oregon’s 2008 Lottery”

--------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Random-assignment instrumental variables (IV) with an intention-to-treat (ITT) benchmark and a two-stage-least-squares (2SLS) estimator.  

Why it fits:

• The 2008 Oregon lottery is a true randomized encouragement: selection is orthogonal to potential outcomes, but compliance is incomplete (≈60 % of lottery “winners’’ ultimately enroll).  
• We want the causal effect of actual Medicaid coverage, not merely of being selected; the lottery therefore serves as a powerful instrument for coverage.  
• Outcomes are measured once pre-lottery (2007) and once post-lottery (2009), permitting a DID or ANCOVA “lagged-outcome’’ specification to improve precision, but the core identification comes from the random instrument.  

Mathematically:  
Stage 1 Medicaid_i,2009 = π · Winner_i + γ Y_i,2007 + X_iβ + ε_i  
Stage 2 Outcome_i,2009 = α · ŜMedicaid_i,2009 + γ Y_i,2007 + X_iβ + ν_i  

Standard errors clustered at the sign-up household (the randomization unit).

--------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable (endogenous):  
Medicaid_i,2009 = 1 if the individual ever had coverage under Oregon Health Plan (OHP) in calendar 2009, 0 otherwise.

Instrument (“encouragement’’):  
Winner_i = 1 if the individual’s name was drawn in any of the 2008 lottery waves, 0 otherwise.

Control group:  
Lottery non-winners (Never selected).

Treatment timing:  
t₀ = March–November 2008 (eight lottery draws). Treatment period = calendar-year 2009 outcomes; baseline = 2007 values.

No running variable or cutoff—this is not an RDD.

--------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------
A1 Random Assignment: Winner_i ⟂ (Y(0), Y(1)).  
Plausibility: By design; publicly monitored drawings.

A2 Exclusion Restriction: Winning affects outcomes only through Medicaid coverage (or pathways integral to having Medicaid).  
Plausibility: Generally good, but threatened because caseworkers who process Medicaid also handle SNAP/TANF; we address this below.

A3 Monotonicity: No one loses Medicaid eligibility because they won the lottery (no “defiers’’).  
Plausibility: Administrative rules make this almost certain.

A4 Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): One person’s assignment does not affect another’s outcomes.  
Plausibility: Some within-household spillovers possible; we keep one observation per household in robustness checks.

A5 First-Stage Relevance: π ≠ 0 (lottery strongly raises Medicaid take-up).  
Plausibility: Empirically π ≈ 0.25; F-stat ≫ 10.

--------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification and Remedies
--------------------------------------------------
T1 Administrative Spillovers (violates exclusion).  
 Fix: Report ITT estimates alongside IV; interpret IV as “Medicaid + facilitation of other benefits.’’ Implement sensitivity analysis dropping individuals whose SNAP/TANF application date is ≤14 days after Medicaid application.

T2 Imperfect SSA match (≈15 % unmatched).  
 Fix: Show balance on observables for matched vs. unmatched; re-estimate weighting by inverse probability of match; prove results unchanged.

T3 Non-classical measurement of earnings (self-employment income missed).  
 Fix: Use “any W-2 earnings’’ and “SSA earnings > 0’’ as robustness; Winsorise top 1 %; run median regressions.

--------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast OLS/IV with clustering
library(modelsummary) # nice tables

# 1. Load data ------------------------------------------------------------
df <- read_csv("oregon_lottery_analytic.csv")  # one row per individual

# 2. Variable construction ------------------------------------------------
df <- df %>% 
  mutate(
    winner          = as.numeric(lottery_winner == 1),
    medicaid2009    = as.numeric(medicaid_months_2009 > 0),
    employed2009    = as.numeric(earnings2009 > 0),
    earn_pov2009    = as.numeric(earnings2009 > fed_poverty_line_2009),
    snap2009        = as.numeric(snap_benefit_2009 > 0),
    tanf2009        = as.numeric(tanf_benefit_2009 > 0),
    ssi2009         = as.numeric(ssi_benefit_2009 > 0),
    ssdi2009        = as.numeric(ssdi_benefit_2009 > 0),
    # Controls
    y07             = earnings2007,
    age             = as.numeric(age_2008),
    female          = as.numeric(sex == "F")
  )

# 3. Main specification: 2SLS --------------------------------------------
# Example: effect on any employment, clustering at household_id
est1 <- feols(employed2009 ~ 1 | 0 | medicaid2009 ~ winner + y07 + age + female,
              data = df, cluster = ~ household_id)

# 4. Robustness: ITT and household-level de-duplication -------------------
# ITT
itt1 <- feols(employed2009 ~ winner + y07 + age + female,
              data = df, cluster = ~ household_id)

# Keep one obs per household (first listed)
df_hh <- df %>% group_by(household_id) %>% slice(1) %>% ungroup()
est1_hh <- feols(employed2009 ~ 1 | 0 | medicaid2009 ~ winner + y07 + age + female,
                 data = df_hh, cluster = ~ household_id)

# 5. Summarise ------------------------------------------------------------
modelsummary(list("2SLS" = est1, "ITT" = itt1, "HH-unique 2SLS" = est1_hh),
             gof_omit = "Adj|R2")
```

--------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------
Theory is ambiguous: Medicaid could reduce labor supply by lowering the need to work for employer insurance, but most beneficiaries were previously uninsured and low-income, so substitution effects are small while income effects are modest. Prior evidence (e.g., ACA expansions) shows near-zero labor-supply responses.

Prior expectation:

• Employment: –1 to –2 percentage points (≈2 % relative decline).  
• Annual earnings: –$200 to –$400 (on a baseline ≈$6,000).  
• Probability earnings > FPL: –1 pp.  
• SNAP/TANF take-up: +3 pp each, reflecting facilitated applications.  
• SSI/SSDI: essentially zero within a one-year horizon.

Magnitude roughly equals 0.02–0.05 s.d. across outcomes.

--------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)
--------------------------------------------------
C1 Randomized instrument ………………………… 1  
C2 Strong first stage (>10) ………………………… 1  
C3 Exclusion satisfied (no direct path) ………… 0.5  
C4 Monotonicity (no defiers) ……………………… 1  
C5 No interference / stable weights ……………… 0.5  
Overall 4 / 5 → credible but exclusion and interference require transparent discussion and robustness checks.

--------------------------------------------------

This plan exploits the Oregon lottery’s random assignment, uses administrative data for high-quality outcomes, and embeds multiple validity and robustness checks to support causal inference on Medicaid’s labor-market and safety-net effects.
